The training dynamics of GANs (Generative Adversarial Networks) and the Transformer fundamentally differ in their approach to handling paired components [Goodfellow et al. 2014, pp.1]. 

In GANs, the generator and discriminator are trained simultaneously in an adversarial process, where the generator tries to produce samples that are indistinguishable from real data, and the discriminator tries to correctly distinguish between real and generated samples [Goodfellow et al. 2014, pp.2]. This process can be viewed as a minimax game, where the generator tries to maximize the probability of the discriminator making a mistake, and the discriminator tries to minimize this probability [Goodfellow et al. 2014, pp.1].

On the other hand, the Transformer is based solely on attention mechanisms and does not involve an adversarial process [Vaswani et al. 2017, pp.1]. The Transformer consists of an encoder and a decoder, which are trained together to maximize the likelihood of the target sequence given the input sequence [Vaswani et al. 2017, pp.2]. The training dynamics of the Transformer are more cooperative, where the encoder and decoder work together to produce the best possible translation [Vaswani et al. 2017, pp.8].

In terms of specific differences, GANs typically involve alternating between training the discriminator and the generator, whereas the Transformer trains the encoder and decoder simultaneously [Goodfellow et al. 2014, pp.3]. Additionally, GANs often require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve stable training, whereas the Transformer has been shown to be more robust and easier to train [Vaswani et al. 2017, pp.10].

Overall, while both GANs and the Transformer involve paired components, their training dynamics are fundamentally different, with GANs involving an adversarial process and the Transformer involving a cooperative process [Goodfellow et al. 2014, pp.1] [Vaswani et al. 2017, pp.1].
